articles.title: How Bonding Curve Token Launches Work on Solana — Building JetForge
articles.excerpt: Launching a token on Solana is relatively straightforward. Building a fair, transparent trading experience around that token is a much more interesting engineering challenge. Traditional token launche…
articles.body: Launching a token on Solana is relatively straightforward. Building a fair, transparent trading experience around that token is a much more interesting engineering challenge. Traditional token launches often require creators to configure liquidity pools, manage initial liquidity, and coordinate trading availability. Bonding curve launchpads introduce a different approach: tokens can begin trading through a predefined pricing mechanism before moving to a decentralized exchange. At JetForge, we're building a Solana token launchpad around this model, with bonding curve trading, token discovery, creator tools, and automated Raydium graduation. In this article, we'll explain the underlying mechanics, why graduation matters, and some of the engineering challenges involved.

articles.title: Data Science in Banking: Finding Hard Rules with Shallow Decision Trees
articles.excerpt: Data Science in Banking, Part 1: Finding Hard Rules with Shallow Decision Trees A credit team reviewing an early-arrears model will eventually ask a practical question: which applications does it flag…
articles.body: Data Science in Banking, Part 1: Finding Hard Rules with Shallow Decision Trees A credit team reviewing an early-arrears model will eventually ask a practical question: which applications does it flag, and why? A short rule can make that discussion concrete. It identifies a segment, shows the conditions for entering it, and lets us count the cases that contradict its prediction. The difficult part is earning that simplicity. A threshold can look convincing because it describes the training sample, because it uses information from the future, or because someone kept adjusting it after seeing the test results. A readable rule deserves the same scrutiny as a complicated model.

articles.title: 27 of 66 "fixed" bugs weren't fixed. So I built a way to check.
articles.excerpt: Keerthirajan Senthilkumar Every coding agent I've used ends its work the same way. A tidy summary, a list of files it changed, and some version of "the issue is resolved." It's convincing. It's also s…
articles.body: Keerthirajan Senthilkumar Every coding agent I've used ends its work the same way. A tidy summary, a list of files it changed, and some version of "the issue is resolved." It's convincing. It's also something you mostly have to take on trust, unless you sit down and review every patch yourself, which defeats a good part of the point. I wanted to know how often that trust is deserved. Not on a benchmark, on real code. The answer from my first proper run: agents handed back 66 patches as done, and 27 of them were wrong. This post is about how I measured that, what I found when I tried to get agents to catch each other's mistakes, and the open source tool that came out of it, bugbout . Benchmarks answer a different question There are good public benchmarks for coding agents.

articles.excerpt: Global digital infrastructure faces an imminent threat from CVE-2026-111497, a memory-corruption vulnerability within Brotli decompression libraries. Confirmed by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure…
articles.body: Introduction: The Brotli Decompression Vulnerability—An Active Threat to Critical Infrastructure Global digital infrastructure faces an imminent threat from CVE-2026-111497 , a memory-corruption vulnerability within Brotli decompression libraries. Confirmed by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) as actively exploited, this flaw directly targets systems leveraging Node.js , .NET , and other software dependent on compromised Brotli decoders. The exploitation mechanism is precise: attackers inject maliciously crafted compressed data, exploiting the decoder’s failure to enforce input validation or bounds checking.

articles.title: ISO 42001 e ISO 27001: o que se aproveita e o que é trabalho novo
articles.excerpt: ISO 42001 e ISO 27001: o que se aproveita e o que é trabalho novo O problema Quando uma empresa já tem ISO 27001 e começa a avaliar a ISO 42001, a primeira pergunta costuma ser errada: qual das duas é…
articles.body: ISO 42001 e ISO 27001: o que se aproveita e o que é trabalho novo O problema Quando uma empresa já tem ISO 27001 e começa a avaliar a ISO 42001, a primeira pergunta costuma ser errada: qual das duas é mais importante. A pergunta certa é outra: o que já está pronto e o que precisa ser construído do zero. Sou auditor de sistemas críticos e vejo esse erro de enquadramento travar decisão de orçamento e de prazo com frequência, porque gestor decide pelo nome da norma, não pelo que ela de fato exige. As duas normas seguem a Estrutura Harmonizada da ISO, a mesma base da ISO 9001: contexto da organização na cláusula 4, liderança na 5, planejamento na 6, apoio na 7, operação na 8, avaliação de desempenho na 9 e melhoria na 10. Essa coincidência não é cosmética.

articles.title: ISS astronaut will conduct Canada's 1st spacewalk in 7 years on Oct. 29: Watch it live
articles.excerpt: Joshua Kutryk will venture outside the International Space Station on Oct. 29, on the first spacewalk by a Canadian astronaut in more than seven years. Here's how to watch it live.
articles.body: The next International Space Station (ISS) spacewalk will have more maple-leaf flavor than usual, as a Canadian astronaut will become the first to go outside the orbiting complex in seven years. Canadian Space Agency (CSA) astronaut Joshua Kutryk, who's also a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force, will help the ISS boost its power supply during his first-ever spacewalk on Thursday (Oct. 29). Kutryk will be joined by NASA astronaut Anil Menon, who has done three spacewalks already and also serves as a colonel with the U.S. Space Force . The duo are scheduled to venture outside the orbiting lab at 8 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT), kicking off a spacewalk that will last roughly 6 hours and 45 minutes. You can watch it live here at Space.com , courtesy of NASA, beginning at 6:30 a.m. EDT (1030 GMT).

articles.title: Foreign gadget bans: all the news about the FCC’s clampdown on Chinese tech
articles.excerpt: A gavel prior to an open commission meeting at the FCC. | Photo: Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images What do drones, routers, and Roombas have in common? The US government wants to keep Chinese ones f…
articles.body: A gavel prior to an open commission meeting at the FCC. | Photo: Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images What do drones , routers , and Roombas have in common? The US government wants to keep Chinese ones from entering the country. They’re the first consumer gadgets that are facing de facto import bans because of the US government’s xenophobic stance — and they might not be the last. Originally, the US government was just worried about US networks. It’s been distrustful of Chinese telecom equipment providers Huawei and ZTE for well over a decade , eventually requiring telecom providers to “rip and replace” their gear . (Many telecoms have still failed to do so .) It established an “Entity List” for companies whose gear should be banned from import, marketing, and sale.

articles.title: Satellites watch an escaping Antarctic iceberg | Space photo of the day for Oct. 28, 2026
articles.excerpt: Iceberg A-81 escaping the Weddell Sea and drifting near the edge of South Georgia's underwater shelf.
articles.body: Iceberg A-81 escaping the Weddell Sea and drifting near the edge of South Georgia's underwater shelf. The image was captured on Oct. 20, 2026. (Image credit: NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison) An iceberg has quickly escaped from the Weddell Sea in Antarctica, on its way to an icy new destination. What is it? As captured by a satellite in orbit, the Antarctic iceberg A-81 has quite quickly (for an iceberg) parted ways from its icy home, breaking off to drift toward a shallow underwater shelf in Georgia. The 600-square-mile (1,550-square-kilometer) iceberg first broke off from the Brunt Ice Shelf in January of 2023. Now, generally speaking, giant icebergs don't travel that fast.

articles.title: Astronomers found a mysterious object beyond Neptune, and it could be a new dwarf planet
articles.excerpt: The Vera Rubin Observatory has discovered a suspected dwarf planet beyond Neptune's orbit. If confirmed, it would be the sixth known dwarf planet in our solar system.
articles.body: The powerful Vera Rubin Observatory has spotted what seems to be a dwarf planet circling the sun in the frigid depths beyond Neptune. The icy object, known as 2026 ED138, is likely between 600 and 1500 kilometers (373 to 972 miles) wide, scientists say. It's therefore probably big enough to be sculpted into a sphere by its own gravity — a key characteristic that separates dwarf planets from asteroids and other small space rocks. And if 2026 ED138 is indeed a dwarf planet, that's a pretty big deal, as astronomers have confirmed just five of them to date: Pluto , Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake .
